slides.title: How a DNS lookup works
bullets: Follow a name from the browser to its IP address
slides.notes: In this chapter we follow one domain name from your browser all the way to an IP address. We meet the servers that take part, the records they return, and the caches that make most lookups almost instant. By the end you can explain why a DNS change seems to take time to spread.

slides.title: The phone book of the internet
slides.quote: The Domain Name System (DNS) is the phone book of the internet.
slides.notes: This short line captures the whole idea of DNS. A phone book turns a name you remember into a number you can dial. DNS does the same job for computers: it turns a domain name into an address they can reach.

slides.title: Names for people, addresses for computers
bullets: People remember names such as example.com
Computers route traffic by IP address, such as 93.184.216.34
DNS (Domain Name System): the lookup service between them
DNS turns a domain name into an IP address
slides.notes: You type a name, but the network cannot route a name. Traffic moves between IP addresses, which are numbers. DNS is the service that sits in between and answers the question: which IP address belongs to this name?

slides.title: Four kinds of server work together
bullets: Each server knows one part of the answer
13 root server names, a to m
Each root name runs on many machines worldwide

rows: Does the legwork of finding the answer
Knows the servers for each top-level domain
Knows the authoritative servers for each domain
Holds the domain's records, gives the final answer

slides.notes: A lookup involves four kinds of server. The recursive resolver is usually run by your internet provider or a public service, and it does the work for you. The root and TLD servers only point onward, and the authoritative name server holds the actual records. The 13 root server names run from a.root-servers.net to m.root-servers.net, and each one is served from many machines around the world.

slides.title: The steps of an uncached lookup

visual.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant device as Your device
  participant resolver as Recursive resolver
  participant root as Root server
  participant tld as TLD server
  participant auth as Authoritative server
  device->>resolver: www.example.com?
  resolver->>root: www.example.com?
  root-->>resolver: Ask the .com servers
  resolver->>tld: www.example.com?
  tld-->>resolver: Ask example.com servers
  resolver->>auth: www.example.com?
  auth-->>resolver: 93.184.216.34
  resolver-->>device: 93.184.216.34
visual.caption: Nothing is cached yet, so the resolver asks three servers

slides.notes: Your device, called the stub resolver, asks the recursive resolver for www.example.com. The resolver asks a root server, which sends it to the .com servers, and a .com TLD server sends it to the name servers of example.com. The authoritative server answers with the IP address, and the resolver returns it to your device and keeps a copy.

slides.title: Recursive versus iterative queries
left: Recursive query: your device to the resolver
Your device is the stub resolver
right: Iterative queries: the resolver to each server
Each answer is a referral onward
The last server gives the address
slides.notes: Two kinds of question happen in one lookup. Your device asks a recursive query: it asks once and expects the finished answer. The resolver then asks iterative queries, and each server replies with a referral to the next server until the authoritative server gives the address.

slides.title: DNS travels over UDP port 53
bullets: Most DNS questions use UDP on port 53
A response too large for UDP is resent over TCP

visual.code:
flowchart LR
  ask["DNS question"] --> udp["UDP port 53"]
  udp --> fits{"Response fits UDP?"}
  fits -- Yes --> answer["Answer received"]
  fits -- No --> tcp["Resent over TCP"]
  tcp --> answer
visual.caption: UDP first, TCP only for large responses

slides.notes: DNS questions are small, so most of them travel over UDP on port 53. When a response is too large to fit, it is sent again over TCP. As a developer, port 53 is the one to remember when you debug DNS traffic.

slides.title: Watch a lookup with dig
bullets: +short prints only the address
+trace shows every referral from the root down

code.content:
dig www.example.com A +short
dig www.example.com A +trace

slides.notes: Try these two commands in a terminal. The first prints just the IP address for www.example.com. The second walks the lookup yourself, showing the root, TLD and authoritative steps we just saw in the diagram.

slides.title: Answers come as resource records
bullets: Resource record: one piece of DNS data
Each has a name, type, TTL and value
The type says what the value holds

rows: Free text, often proof of ownership

slides.notes: The authoritative server answers with resource records. Every record has a name, a type, a time to live and a value. The A record is the one our lookup asked for, but you will meet the other types when you set up mail, aliases or prove you own a domain.

slides.title: TTL says how long a copy lasts
bullets: TTL (time to live): reuse time in seconds
Every answer is cached for its TTL
Caching avoids asking four servers every time
slides.notes: Asking four servers for every name would be slow, so every answer is cached. The TTL tells each cache how many seconds it may reuse its copy. Remember that TTL is always in seconds: 3600 means one hour, not one hour and some minutes.

slides.title: A lookup stops at the first fresh copy
bullets: Copies live in three places
Browser, operating system, recursive resolver
A full lookup runs only when all miss

visual.caption: Each cache is checked in turn

slides.notes: Before any server is asked, the browser checks its own cache, then the operating system checks its cache. If both miss, the recursive resolver checks its cache. Only when every copy is missing or expired does the resolver walk from the root down.

slides.title: Short TTL or long TTL
left: More questions to the authoritative server
right: Less traffic to the authoritative server
Old copies served until TTL runs out
slides.notes: Choosing a TTL is a trade-off. A short TTL lets a change reach users quickly but sends more questions to the authoritative server. A long TTL cuts that traffic, but old copies stay in caches until their TTL runs out, which is why a DNS change seems to take time to propagate.

slides.title: How much caching saves

visual.caption: Example timings in milliseconds; uncached is root 20 + TLD 30 + authoritative 40

slides.notes: Here is one example lookup in milliseconds. Uncached, the resolver spends 20 ms at the root, 30 ms at the TLD server and 40 ms at the authoritative server, 90 ms in total. A moment later the same answer comes from the resolver's cache in about 1 ms.

slides.title: What to remember
bullets: DNS turns a domain name into an IP address
Resolver asks root, then TLD, then authoritative server
Answers are resource records with a name, type, TTL, value
Browser, OS and resolver cache answers for the TTL
TTL trades fast changes against fewer queries
slides.notes: Let's recap the chapter. A lookup follows a fixed path from root to TLD to authoritative server, and the answer comes back as resource records. Caching in three places makes most lookups take about a millisecond, and the TTL decides how long those copies live.
